claim: Treatment with IFN-γ and LPS, but neither agent alone, led to the initiation of a robust DDR in BMDMs.
source: Treatment with IFN-γ and the TLR4 agonist, LPS, but neither agent alone, led to the initiation of a robust DDR in BMDMs (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing γ-H2AX and p-KAP-1 formation only when both IFN-γ and LPS are present (Figure 1A).

claim: Infection of BMDMs with L. monocytogenes led to a robust DDR.
source: Infection of BMDMs with the intracellular bacterial pathogen L. monocytogenes also led to a robust DDR, and IFN-γ augments, but is not required for, this response (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing γ-H2AX and p-KAP-1 formation after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 1B).

claim: IFN-γ augments, but is not required for, the DDR in L. monocytogenes-infected BMDMs.
source: Infection of BMDMs with the intracellular bacterial pathogen L. monocytogenes also led to a robust DDR, and IFN-γ augments, but is not required for, this response (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing DDR occurs with L. monocytogenes infection alone, with enhancement when IFN-γ is added (Figure 1B).

claim: LPS and IFN-γ treatment of primary peritoneal macrophages activates a robust DDR.
source: As with cultured BMDMs, LPS and IFN-γ treatment of primary macrophages isolated from the peritoneal cavity also activates a robust DDR (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing γ-H2AX and p-KAP-1 formation in primary peritoneal macrophages (Figure 1C).

claim: ATM is activated in BMDMs, as evidenced by the loss of KAP-1 phosphorylation in ATM-deficient BMDMs.
source: ATM is activated in BMDMs, as evidenced by the loss of KAP-1 phosphorylation in ATM-deficient (Atm-/-) BMDMs treated with LPS and IFN-γ or infected with L. monocytogenes (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing absence of p-KAP-1 in Atm-/- BMDMs (Figures 1D and 1E).

claim: Both ATM and DNA-PKcs are activated in response to LPS and IFN-γ in BMDMs.
source: Inhibition of DNA-PKcs kinase activity in Atm-/-BMDMs, however, abrogated H2AX phosphorylation in response to LPS and IFN-γ, demonstrating that both ATM and DNA-PKcs are activated in response to LPS and IFN-γ (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing that inhibition of DNA-PKcs in Atm-/- BMDMs eliminates γ-H2AX formation (Figure 1F).

claim: BMDMs deficient in both ATM and DNA-PKcs exhibit a near-complete abrogation of γ-H2AX and p-KAP-1 formation in response to L. monocytogenes infection.
source: Whereas BMDMs with isolated deficiencies of ATM or DNA-PKcs exhibit a robust DDR, those with deficiencies in both ATM and DNA-PKcs (Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+) exhibit a near-complete abrogation of γ-H2AX and p-KAP-1 formation in response to infection with L. monocytogenes (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing minimal γ-H2AX and p-KAP-1 in Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 1H).

claim: Both uninfected Lyz2Cre/+ and Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs are cycling.
source: Though uninfected Lyz2Cre/+ and Scid:Atm C/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDM are cycling, both undergo G1 arrest after infection with L. monocytogenes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis of BrdU incorporation and DNA content (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Both Lyz2Cre/+ and Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs undergo G1 arrest after infection with L. monocytogenes.
source: Though uninfected Lyz2Cre/+ and Scid:Atm C/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDM are cycling, both undergo G1 arrest after infection with L. monocytogenes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis showing cell cycle arrest after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs can have unique or overlapping functions in the DDR.
source: We conclude that both ATM and DNA-PKcs are activated in BMDMs by LPS and IFN-γ or infection with L. monocytogenes, and that these kinases can have unique (ATM phosphorylation of KAP-1) or overlapping (ATM or DNA-PKcs phosphorylation of H2AX) functions.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of ATM and DNA-PKcs deficiency on KAP-1 versus H2AX phosphorylation shown in Figures 1D-H.

claim: There is a significant increase in the Olive Tail Moment in BMDMs after infection with L. monocytogenes or treatment with LPS and IFN-γ.
source: The neutral comet assay, which quantifies genomic DSBs in single cells, revealed a significant increase in the Olive Tail Moment (measure of DNA DSBs) in BMDM after infection with L. monocytogenes or treatment with LPS and IFN-γ (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by neutral comet assay data showing increased Olive Tail Moment (Figure 2A).

claim: BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes exhibit an increase in γ-H2AX nuclear foci relative to uninfected cells.
source: BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes exhibit an increase in γ-H2AX nuclear foci relative to uninfected cells, indicative of genomic DNA DSB formation (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing γ-H2AX foci in infected BMDMs (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Infection of DNA Ligase IV-deficient BMDMs with L. monocytogenes leads to augmented γ-H2AX formation compared to control BMDMs.
source: As compared to Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs (normal NHEJ), infection of Lig4loxP/loxP:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs (loss of NHEJ) with L. monocytogenes leads to augmented γ-H2AX formation (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing increased γ-H2AX in DNA Ligase IV-deficient BMDMs (Figure 2C).

claim: Mre11ATLD1/ATLD1 BMDMs exhibit a significant reduction in ATM-dependent phosphorylation of KAP-1 in response to LPS and IFN-γ.
source: Mice homozygous for a hypomorphic Mre11 allele (Mre11ATLD1/ATLD1) exhibit diminished ATM activation in response to DNA DSBs, and BMDMs derived from these mice exhibit a significant reduction in the ATM-dependent phosphorylation of KAP-1 in response to LPS and IFN-γ (Figure 2D) (Theunissen et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing reduced p-KAP-1 in Mre11ATLD1/ATLD1 BMDMs (Figure 2D) and citation to prior work on Mre11 function.

claim: The initiation of a DDR in activated macrophages occurs primarily through the generation of genomic DNA DSBs.
source: Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the initiation of a DDR in activated macrophages occurs primarily through the generation of genomic DNA DSBs.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including comet assays, γ-H2AX foci, and effects of DNA repair deficiency (Figures 2A-D).

claim: Treatment with AGHS, but not MnTMPyP, prevented γ-H2AX formation in response to LPS and IFN-γ.
source: Treatment with AGHS, but not MnTMPyP, prevented γ-H2AX formation in response to LPS and IFN-γ, suggesting that NO, and not ROS, initiates DDR in activated BMDMs (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing that AGHS (NOS inhibitor) but not MnTMPyP (ROS scavenger) blocks γ-H2AX formation (Figure 2E).

claim: NO, and not ROS, initiates DDR in activated BMDMs.
source: Treatment with AGHS, but not MnTMPyP, prevented γ-H2AX formation in response to LPS and IFN-γ, suggesting that NO, and not ROS, initiates DDR in activated BMDMs (Figure 2E).
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of NOS inhibitor versus ROS scavenger on DDR (Figure 2E).

claim: BMDMs deficient in nitric oxide synthase (Nos2-/-) exhibit diminished γ-H2AX in response to LPS and IFN-γ.
source: In agreement with this finding, BMDMs deficient in the nitric oxide synthase (Nos2-/-) exhibit diminished γ-H2AX in response to LPS and IFN-γ, whereas loss of gp91phox (Nox2-/-), an essential catalytic subunit of the NADPH oxidase, has no effect on γ-H2AX formation (Figure 2F) (Laubach et al., 1995; Pollock et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing reduced γ-H2AX in Nos2-/- BMDMs (Figure 2F) and citations to prior work on Nos2 and Nox2.

claim: Loss of gp91phox (Nox2-/-) has no effect on γ-H2AX formation in response to LPS and IFN-γ.
source: In agreement with this finding, BMDMs deficient in the nitric oxide synthase (Nos2-/-) exhibit diminished γ-H2AX in response to LPS and IFN-γ, whereas loss of gp91phox (Nox2-/-), an essential catalytic subunit of the NADPH oxidase, has no effect on γ-H2AX formation (Figure 2F) (Laubach et al., 1995; Pollock et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing normal γ-H2AX in Nox2-/- BMDMs (Figure 2F) and citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of the DDR in macrophages depends on NO production.
source: Thus, activation of the DDR in macrophages depends on NO production.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of NOS inhibition and Nos2 deficiency on DDR (Figures 2E-F).

claim: After infection of BMDMs with L. monocytogenes, DDR activation depends on TLR signaling.
source: Indeed, after infection of BMDMs with L. monocytogenes, DDR activation depends on TLR signaling, as BMDMs deficient in MyD88, a critical TLR adaptor protein, exhibit diminished γ-H2AX formation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing reduced γ-H2AX in Myd88-/- BMDMs after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 3A).

claim: Heat-killed L. monocytogenes does not initiate a DDR in the absence of exogenous IFN.
source: In agreement with this notion, heat-killed L. monocytogenes, which activates TLR signaling but does not enter the cytosol and stimulate type I IFN production, does not initiate a DDR in the absence of exogenous IFN (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no γ-H2AX with heat-killed L. monocytogenes alone (Figure 3B).

claim: BMDMs deficient in STING (Tmem173-/-) do not initiate a DDR after infection with L. monocytogenes.
source: Moreover, BMDMs deficient in STING (Tmem173-/-), a cytosolic protein required to stimulate type I IFN production downstream of L. monocytogenes DNA, do not initiate a DDR after infection with L. monocytogenes (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no γ-H2AX or p-KAP-1 in Tmem173-/- BMDMs after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 3C).

claim: DDR signaling is not observed in type I IFN receptor-deficient (Ifnar1-/-) BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes.
source: Finally, DDR signaling is not observed in type I IFN receptor-deficient (Ifnar1-/-) BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no γ-H2AX or p-KAP-1 in Ifnar1-/- BMDMs after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 3D).

claim: Ifnar1-/- BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes do not produce NO.
source: Though Ifnar1-/- BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes do not produce NO, addition of IFN-γ rescues NO production to wild type levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by nitrite concentration measurements in culture supernatants (Figure 4A).

claim: Addition of IFN-γ rescues NO production to wild type levels in Ifnar1-/- BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes.
source: Though Ifnar1-/- BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes do not produce NO, addition of IFN-γ rescues NO production to wild type levels (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by nitrite concentration measurements showing rescue of NO production with IFN-γ (Figure 4A).

claim: Addition of IFN-γ to Ifnar1-/- BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes does not lead to a robust DDR despite rescuing NO production.
source: This, however, does not lead to a robust DDR (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing minimal γ-H2AX and p-KAP-1 in Ifnar1-/- BMDMs even with IFN-γ addition (Figure 4B).

claim: Type I IFN signaling is required to promote the DDR in BMDMs beyond its role in stimulating NO production.
source: Thus, type I IFN signaling is required to promote the DDR in BMDMs beyond its role in stimulating NO production.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IFN-γ rescues NO production but not DDR in Ifnar1-/- BMDMs (Figures 4A-B).

claim: Type I IFN does not augment DNA DSB generation in BMDMs treated with bleomycin.
source: Type I IFN does not augment DNA DSB generation, as evidenced by the equivalent levels of DNA DSBs observed by neutral comet assay analysis of BMDMs treated with the DNA DSB-inducing agent bleomycin in the presence or absence of type I IFN (IFN-β) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by neutral comet assay data showing no difference in Olive Tail Moment with or without IFN-β (Figure 4C).

claim: A robust DDR to bleomycin is only observed in BMDMs treated with IFN-β.
source: However, a robust DDR to bleomycin is only observed in BMDMs treated with IFN-β (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing p-KAP-1 only when BMDMs are treated with both bleomycin and IFN-β (Figure 4D).

claim: MEFs treated with bleomycin exhibit a robust DDR that is not augmented by the addition of either IFN-β or IFN-γ.
source: In contrast to macrophages, mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) treated with bleomycin exhibit a robust DDR that is not augmented by the addition of either IFN-β or IFN-γ (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing p-KAP-1 in MEFs with bleomycin alone (Figures 4D and 4E).

claim: Unlike other cell types, the DDR in macrophages depends on type I IFN signaling.
source: Thus, unlike other cell types, the DDR in macrophages depends on type I IFN signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirement for type I IFN in BMDMs versus MEFs (Figures 4D-E).

claim: Type I IFN signaling does not affect cell cycle parameters in BMDMs.
source: This is not due to an effect of type I IFN signaling on cell cycle parameters or the expression of key DDR proteins (Mre11, Rad50, Nbs1, Ku70, Ku80, ATR, DNA-PKcs, ATM and H2AX) in BMDMs (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis of cell cycle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Type I IFN signaling does not affect the expression of key DDR proteins (Mre11, Rad50, Nbs1, Ku70, Ku80, ATR, DNA-PKcs, ATM and H2AX) in BMDMs.
source: This is not due to an effect of type I IFN signaling on cell cycle parameters or the expression of key DDR proteins (Mre11, Rad50, Nbs1, Ku70, Ku80, ATR, DNA-PKcs, ATM and H2AX) in BMDMs (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing no change in DDR protein expression with IFN-β treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: Many DDR proteins exhibit substantially lower expression in BMDMs as compared to MEFs.
source: Notably, many of these proteins exhibit substantially lower expression in BMDMs as compared to MEFs (see Discussion).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data comparing protein expression between BMDMs and MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: The expression of 322 genes was induced (≥4 fold) after infection of Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs with L. monocytogenes.
source: The expression of 322 genes was induced (≥4 fold) after infection of Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs with L. monocytogenes (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling data (Figure 5A and source data).

claim: 128 genes exhibited greater (≥1.25 fold) induction in Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes relative to infected Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs, indicating that their expression is regulated by ATM and/or DNA-PKcs.
source: Of these, 128 exhibited greater (≥1.25 fold) induction in Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes relative to infected Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs, indicating that their expression is regulated by ATM and/or DNA-PKcs (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling data comparing control and DDR-deficient BMDMs (Figure 5A and source data).

claim: DDR-regulated genes encode proteins with diverse functions in the immune response, including cytokines, chemokines, and cell surface proteins.
source: These genes encode proteins with diverse functions in the immune response, including several cytokines, chemokines, and cell surface proteins such as the class A scavenger receptor MARCO and CD69, which has a role in cell localization and migration (Figure 5A and B) (Kraal et al., 2000; Schwab and Cyster, 2007).
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling data and citations to prior work on MARCO and CD69 function.

claim: The DDR in L. monocytogenes-infected BMDMs regulates the expression of many (Cxcl1, Cxcl10, Ccl2, Ccl3 and Ccl4), but not all (Ccl5), chemokine genes.
source: The DDR in L. monocytogenes-infected BMDMs regulates the expression of many (Cxcl1, Cxcl10, Ccl2, Ccl3 and Ccl4), but not all (Ccl5), chemokine genes that are induced in activated macrophages (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling and qRT-PCR data (Figures 5A and 5B).

claim: Both ATM and DNA-PKcs can function to regulate gene expression in some cases (Marco and Cxcl10).
source: The analysis of BMDMs deficient in ATM (Atm-/-) or DNA-PKcs (Scid) revealed that both of these kinases can function to regulate gene expression (Figure 5C, Marco and Cxcl10), whereas in other cases the activity of either of these kinases is adequate (Figure 5C, Ccl2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing reduced expression in both Atm-/- and Scid BMDMs for some genes (Figure 5C).

claim: For some genes (Ccl2), the activity of either ATM or DNA-PKcs is adequate to regulate expression.
source: The analysis of BMDMs deficient in ATM (Atm-/-) or DNA-PKcs (Scid) revealed that both of these kinases can function to regulate gene expression (Figure 5C, Marco and Cxcl10), whereas in other cases the activity of either of these kinases is adequate (Figure 5C, Ccl2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing normal expression in single-deficient BMDMs for some genes (Figure 5C).

claim: Once activated by DNA DSBs, ATM and DNA-PKcs regulate the functional genetic program of activated macrophages.
source: We conclude that once activated by DNA DSBs, ATM and DNA-PKcs regulate the functional genetic program of activated macrophages.
evidence: Inferred from gene expression profiling data showing DDR-dependent regulation of immune genes (Figures 5A-C).

claim: Loss of both ATM and DNA-PKcs leads to a significant reduction in IL-1β production in response to infection of BMDMs with L. monocytogenes.
source: Loss of both ATM and DNA-PKcs (Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+) leads to a significant reduction in IL-1β production in response to infection of BMDMs with L. monocytogenes (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-1β in Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs (Figure 6A).

claim: BMDMs with isolated deficiencies in ATM or DNA-PKcs exhibit only a mild reduction in IL-1β production.
source: In contrast, BMDMs with isolated deficiencies in ATM or DNA-PKcs exhibit only a mild reduction in IL-1β production (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as observation from unpublished data.

claim: There are no notable differences in ROS levels among the different macrophages examined.
source: However, we do not observe any notable differences in ROS levels among the different macrophages examined here (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis of mitochondrial superoxide levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs are not required to promote pro-IL-1β gene expression.
source: ATM and DNA-PKcs are not required to promote pro-IL-1β gene expression, nor are they required for optimal expression of the Asc, Nlrp3, or Aim2 genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing no difference in pro-IL-1β, Asc, Nlrp3, or Aim2 expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs are not required for optimal expression of the Asc, Nlrp3, or Aim2 genes.
source: ATM and DNA-PKcs are not required to promote pro-IL-1β gene expression, nor are they required for optimal expression of the Asc, Nlrp3, or Aim2 genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: After infection with L. monocytogenes, Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs are unable to efficiently convert inactive pro-caspase 1 to active caspase 1 (p20).
source: Rather, after infection with L. monocytogenes, Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs are unable to efficiently convert inactive pro-caspase 1 to active caspase 1 (p20) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing reduced caspase 1 p20 in Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs (Figure 6B).

claim: AIM2 inflammasome activation by LPS and poly dA:dT depends on an intact DDR.
source: This requirement for ATM and DNA-PKcs is not specific to L. monocytogenes, as AIM2 inflammasome activation by LPS and poly dA:dT also depends on an intact DDR (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-1β in Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs treated with LPS and poly dA:dT (Figure 6C).

claim: Activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome with LPS and either nigericin or MSU crystals is defective in Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs.
source: Moreover, activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome with LPS and either nigericin or monosodium urate (MSU) crystals is also defective in Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs as evidenced by reduced IL-1β production in response to these stimuli (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-1β in Scid:AtmC/C:Lyz2Cre/+ BMDMs treated with LPS and nigericin or MSU (Figure 6D).

claim: Production of IL-18 relies primarily on DNA-PKcs.
source: In contrast to IL-1β, production of IL-18 relies primarily on DNA-PKcs, as Scid BMDMs produce significantly less IL-18 after L. monocytogenes infection (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-18 in Scid BMDMs (Figure 7A).

claim: DNA-PKcs is not required to promote pro-IL-18 gene expression.
source: DNA-PKcs is not required to promote pro-IL-18 gene expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing no difference in pro-IL-18 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Scid BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes were not effective at stimulating IFN-γ production by co-cultured NK cells.
source: As compared to wild type BMDMs, Scid BMDMs infected with L. monocytogenes were not effective at simulating IFN-γ production by co-cultured NK cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis of intracellular IFN-γ in NK cells (Figure 7B).

claim: Scid and wild type BMDMs both induce IL-12 (p40) gene expression upon infection with L. monocytogenes.
source: Scid and wild type BMDMs both induce IL-12 (p40) gene expression upon infection with L. monocytogenes and the addition of exogenous IL-18 rescues IFN-γ production by NK cells co-cultured with L. monocytogenes-infected Scid BMDMs (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data showing similar IL-12p40 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Addition of exogenous IL-18 rescues IFN-γ production by NK cells co-cultured with L. monocytogenes-infected Scid BMDMs.
source: Scid and wild type BMDMs both induce IL-12 (p40) gene expression upon infection with L. monocytogenes and the addition of exogenous IL-18 rescues IFN-γ production by NK cells co-cultured with L. monocytogenes-infected Scid BMDMs (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis showing rescue of IFN-γ production with IL-18 addition (Figure 7B).

claim: The inability of Scid BMDMs to induce NK cells to make IFN-γ is due to the role of DNA-PKcs stimulating IL-18 production.
source: Thus, the inability of Scid BMDMs to induce NK cells to make IFN-γ is due to the role of DNA-PKcs stimulating IL-18 production.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that IL-18 addition rescues IFN-γ production and Scid BMDMs have reduced IL-18 (Figures 7A-B).

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs regulate inflammasome function in response to a broad variety of activators.
source: We concluded that ATM and DNA-PKcs regulate inflammasome function in response to a broad variety of activators.
evidence: Inferred from data showing DDR effects on multiple inflammasome activators (Figures 6C-D).

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs are differentially required for the production of IL-1β and IL-18 by the inflammasome.
source: Moreover, these two kinases are differentially required for the production of IL-1β and IL-18 by the inflammasome.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects on IL-1β (requires both kinases) versus IL-18 (primarily DNA-PKcs) (Figures 6A, 7A).

claim: Macrophages produce genotoxic agents, such as reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, that kill invading pathogens.
source: Macrophages produce genotoxic agents, such as reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, that kill invading pathogens.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about macrophage antimicrobial mechanisms.

claim: Genotoxic agents activate the DDR kinases ATM and DNA-PKcs through the generation of double stranded breaks (DSBs) in murine macrophage genomic DNA.
source: Here we show that these agents activate the DNA damage response (DDR) kinases ATM and DNA-PKcs through the generation of double stranded breaks (DSBs) in murine macrophage genomic DNA.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental approaches including comet assays, immunofluorescence, and genetic studies (Figures 1-2).

claim: Initiation of the DDR in macrophages depends on signaling from the type I interferon receptor.
source: In contrast to other cell types, initiation of this DDR depends on signaling from the type I interferon receptor.
evidence: Supported by experiments with Ifnar1-/- BMDMs and comparison to MEFs (Figures 3-4).

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs regulate a genetic program with diverse immune functions in macrophages.
source: Once activated, ATM and DNA-PKcs regulate a genetic program with diverse immune functions and promote inflammasome activation and the production of IL-1β and IL-18.
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling and functional assays (Figures 5-7).

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs promote inflammasome activation and the production of IL-1β and IL-18 in macrophages.
source: Once activated, ATM and DNA-PKcs regulate a genetic program with diverse immune functions and promote inflammasome activation and the production of IL-1β and IL-18.
evidence: Supported by ELISA and Western blot data showing reduced cytokine production and caspase-1 activation in DDR-deficient BMDMs (Figures 6-7).

claim: Following infection with L. monocytogenes, DNA-PKcs-deficient murine macrophages produce reduced levels of IL-18.
source: Indeed, following infection with Listeria monocytogenes, DNA-PKcs-deficient murine macrophages produce reduced levels of IL-18 and are unable to optimally stimulate IFN-γ production by NK cells.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-18 in Scid BMDMs (Figure 7A).

claim: DNA-PKcs-deficient murine macrophages are unable to optimally stimulate IFN-γ production by NK cells following infection with L. monocytogenes.
source: Indeed, following infection with Listeria monocytogenes, DNA-PKcs-deficient murine macrophages produce reduced levels of IL-18 and are unable to optimally stimulate IFN-γ production by NK cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis of NK cell IFN-γ production (Figure 7B).

claim: Genomic DNA DSBs act as signaling intermediates in murine macrophages, regulating innate immune responses through the initiation of a type I IFN-dependent DDR.
source: Thus, genomic DNA DSBs act as signaling intermediates in murine macrophages, regulating innate immune responses through the initiation of a type I IFN-dependent DDR.
evidence: Inferred from the collective findings showing DSB generation, type I IFN requirement, and downstream immune effects (Figures 1-7).

claim: DNA DSBs are a dangerous form of DNA damage which, if incorrectly repaired, lead to chromosomal rearrangements and genome instability.
source: DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) are a dangerous form of DNA damage which, if incorrectly repaired, lead to chromosomal rearrangements and genome instability (Jackson and Bartek, 2009).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: Cells mount a canonical DNA damage response (DDR) to repair DSBs and protect the integrity of the genome.
source: Cells mount a canonical DNA damage response (DDR) to repair DSBs and protect the integrity of the genome (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: In G1-phase cells, the DDR is initiated through the activation of ATM and DNA-PKcs.
source: In G1-phase cells, this DDR is initiated through the activation of ataxia telangiectasia mutated (ATM) and the catalytic subunit of the DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PKcs), both members of the PI3-like family of serine threonine kinases (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs phosphorylate downstream targets that drive the cellular response to DNA damage.
source: These kinases phosphorylate downstream targets that drive the cellular response to DNA damage (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: ATM is the primary kinase that orchestrates the DDR in G1-phase cells.
source: ATM is the primary kinase that orchestrates the DDR in G1-phase cells (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: DNA-PKcs has fewer known DDR functions than ATM, but shares some downstream targets and functions with ATM.
source: DNA-PKcs, by contrast, has fewer known DDR functions, but shares some downstream targets, and functions, with ATM (Callén et al., 2009).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: The canonical DDR includes the activation of cell cycle checkpoints and the initiation of DSB repair by NHEJ in G1-phase cells.
source: The canonical DDR includes the activation of cell cycle checkpoints and, in G1-phase cells, the initiation of DSB repair by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: In some contexts, the DDR can regulate non-canonical cell type-specific responses.
source: However, in some contexts, the DDR can regulate non-canonical cell type-specific responses.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge and is supported by subsequent citations to specific examples.

claim: DNA DSBs generated by the RAG endonuclease during antigen receptor gene assembly activate a genetic program important for normal lymphocyte development.
source: DNA DSBs generated by the RAG endonuclease during antigen receptor gene assembly activate a genetic program that is important for normal lymphocyte development (Bednarski et al., 2012, 2016; Bredemeyer et al., 2008; Helmink and Sleckman, 2012).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: DNA damaging agents can induce components of the lymphocyte genetic program in developing lymphocytes.
source: DNA damaging agents can also induce components of this genetic program in developing lymphocytes (Bredemeyer et al., 2008; Innes et al., 2013).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: DNA DSBs generated during immunoglobulin class switch recombination in mature B cells induce gene expression changes required for plasma cell differentiation.
source: DNA DSBs generated during immunoglobulin class switch recombination in mature B cells induce gene expression changes required for plasma cell differentiation (Sherman et al., 2010).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: RAG activity in lymphoid progenitors alters the function of mature T and NK cells, presumably through the generation of DSBs and activation of the DDR.
source: RAG activity in lymphoid progenitors alters the function of mature T and NK cells, presumably through the generation of DSBs and activation of the DDR in these cells (Karo et al., 2014).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text, with speculative interpretation.

claim: DDR activated by replication stress can promote the differentiation of polyploid macrophages that have developed in response to chronic inflammatory stimuli.
source: Additionally, DDR activated by replication stress can promote the differentiation of polyploid macrophages that have developed in response to chronic inflammatory stimuli (Herrtwich et al., 2016).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: Innate immune cells such as macrophages are among the first to respond to bacterial pathogens.
source: Innate immune cells such as macrophages are among the first to respond to bacterial pathogens.
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge.

claim: Macrophages are activated by signals from Toll-like receptors (TLRs) that bind bacterial ligands and by interferon receptor signals.
source: They are activated by signals from Toll-like receptors (TLRs) that bind bacterial ligands and by interferon (IFN, type I or II) receptor signals (Akira and Takeda, 2004; McNab et al., 2015; Schoenborn and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: Bacterial pathogens that enter the cytosol, such as L. monocytogenes, activate cytosolic pathways that lead to the production of type I IFN and inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 through activation of the inflammasome.
source: Bacterial pathogens that enter the cytosol, such as Listeria monocytogenes, activate additional cytosolic pathways that lead to the production of type I IFN and the production of inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 through activation of the inflammasome (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014; McNab et al., 2015; Witte et al., 2012).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: Once activated, macrophages produce genotoxic agents that kill bacterial pathogens, including ROS and NO.
source: Once activated, macrophages produce genotoxic agents that kill bacterial pathogens, including reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reactive nitrogen species such as nitric oxide (NO) (Mosser and Edwards, 2008).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: ROS is generated rapidly through the activation of the NADPH oxidase.
source: ROS is generated rapidly through the activation of the NADPH oxidase.
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge.

claim: NO production is delayed due to a requirement to induce the expression of the Nos2 gene.
source: NO production, by contrast, is delayed due to a requirement to induce the expression of the Nos2 gene, which encodes the nitric oxide synthase (MacMicking et al., 1997).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: Nos2 expression is induced by TLR signals coupled with IFN receptor (type I or II) signals.
source: Nos2 expression is induced by TLR signals coupled with IFN receptor (type I or II) signals.
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge.

claim: Both ROS and NO have genotoxic properties and could conceivably damage host macrophage genomic DNA.
source: Both ROS and NO have genotoxic properties and could conceivably damage host macrophage genomic DNA, initiating a DDR that could regulate macrophage functions in innate immune responses.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about genotoxic properties of ROS and NO, with speculative extension to macrophage function.

claim: The DDR is an important signaling pathway in innate immune responses.
source: These findings establish the DDR as an important signaling pathway in innate immune responses.
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Entry of L. monocytogenes into the cytosol activates the NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes.
source: Entry of L. monocytogenes into the cytosol activates the NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes, leading to the activation of the caspase 1 protease and cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 to form active IL-1β and IL-18, respectively (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014; von Moltke et al., 2013; Witte et al., 2012).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: Inflammasome activation leads to the activation of the caspase 1 protease and cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 to form active IL-1β and IL-18.
source: Entry of L. monocytogenes into the cytosol activates the NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes, leading to the activation of the caspase 1 protease and cleavage of pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 to form active IL-1β and IL-18, respectively (Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2014; von Moltke et al., 2013; Witte et al., 2012).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: IL-12 and IL-18 stimulate T cells and NK cells to produce IFN-γ.
source: IL-12 and IL-18 stimulate T cells and NK cells to produce IFN-γ (Akira, 2000; Hsieh et al., 1993; Okamura et al., 1995).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: Most bacteria initiate TLR signals and stimulate type I IFN production, leading to NO production.
source: Most bacteria initiate TLR signals and stimulate type I IFN production, leading to NO production, which should generate DNA DSBs and activate a DDR in macrophages.
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge with inference about DDR activation.

claim: The DDR will be activated, and regulate macrophage functions, in response to a broad variety of bacterial pathogens and other activating stimuli.
source: Thus, we reason that the DDR will be activated, and regulate macrophage functions, in response to a broad variety of bacterial pathogens and other activating stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the findings with L. monocytogenes and other inflammasome activators.

claim: ROS initiates a DDR in a human cervical cell line infected with Chlamydia trachomatis.
source: In this regard, ROS initiates a DDR in a human cervical cell line infected with the intracellular pathogen Chlamydia trachomatis (Chumduri et al., 2013).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: ROS is produced immediately upon macrophage activation.
source: Whereas ROS is produced immediately upon macrophage activation, NO production is delayed due to the requirement for induction of Nos2 gene expression and production of nitric oxide synthase (MacMicking et al., 1997; Nunes et al., 2013).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: NO production is delayed relative to ROS production due to the requirement for induction of Nos2 gene expression and production of nitric oxide synthase.
source: Whereas ROS is produced immediately upon macrophage activation, NO production is delayed due to the requirement for induction of Nos2 gene expression and production of nitric oxide synthase (MacMicking et al., 1997; Nunes et al., 2013).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: NO-induced DNA damage, the initiation of a DDR, and its physiologic effects on macrophage function will be delayed relative to macrophage activation.
source: Thus, NO-induced DNA damage, the initiation of a DDR, and its physiologic effects on macrophage function will be delayed relative to macrophage activation.
evidence: Inferred from the delayed production of NO and its role in initiating DDR.

claim: NO can react with other species, giving rise to agents such as N2O3, which can cause DNA crosslinking and strand breaks.
source: Though the mechanism by which NO induces DNA damage remains unclear, NO can react with other species, giving rise to agents such as N2O3, which can cause DNA crosslinking and strand breaks, and the highly reactive peroxynitrite, which rapidly reacts with DNA and can cause DNA breaks and mutations (Anand and Stamler, 2012; Radi, 2013; Tamir et al., 1996).
evidence: Draws from established biochemical knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: Peroxynitrite rapidly reacts with DNA and can cause DNA breaks and mutations.
source: Though the mechanism by which NO induces DNA damage remains unclear, NO can react with other species, giving rise to agents such as N2O3, which can cause DNA crosslinking and strand breaks, and the highly reactive peroxynitrite, which rapidly reacts with DNA and can cause DNA breaks and mutations (Anand and Stamler, 2012; Radi, 2013; Tamir et al., 1996).
evidence: Draws from established biochemical knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: It is possible that there are regions within the genome that are more susceptible to genotoxic damage by nitric oxide and its metabolic derivatives.
source: Though these lesions likely occur at random in macrophage DNA, it is certainly possible that there are regions within the genome that are more susceptible to genotoxic damage by nitric oxide and its metabolic derivatives.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential non-random DNA damage.

claim: It is possible that DNA DSBs could be generated, and a DDR initiated, in activated macrophages in the absence of NO.
source: It is possible that DNA DSBs could be generated, and a DDR initiated, in activated macrophages in the absence of NO.
evidence: Speculative statement about alternative mechanisms of DDR activation.

claim: Pathogens can produce agents that can directly or indirectly cause DNA damage.
source: In this regard, pathogens can produce agents that can directly or indirectly cause DNA damage (Guerra et al., 2011; Weitzman and Weitzman, 2014).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: Cytolethal Distending Toxins (CDT), produced by some bacteria, have phosphodiesterase activity and can cause DNA DSBs.
source: Cytolethal Distending Toxins (CDT), produced by some bacteria, have phosphodiesterase activity and can cause DNA DSBs (Alaoui-El-Azher et al., 2010; Fedor et al., 2013; Frisan et al., 2003; Guerra et al., 2011; Jinadasa et al., 2011; Nesić et al., 2004; Weitzman and Weitzman, 2014).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: Some strains of bacteria produce the genotoxic agent colibactin.
source: Some strains of bacteria produce the genotoxic agent colibactin (Cuevas-Ramos et al., 2010; Nougayrède et al., 2006).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: Some bacteria produce agents that can directly modulate the DDR and its activities in response to these pathogens.
source: Moreover, some bacteria produce agents that can directly modulate the DDR and its activities in response to these pathogens (Weitzman and Weitzman, 2014).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: Different bacteria may have evolved ways to induce DNA DSBs and to modulate the DDR.
source: Thus, different bacteria may have evolved ways to induce DNA DSBs and to modulate the DDR.
evidence: Inferred from the cited examples of bacterial toxins and agents that affect DNA damage and DDR.

claim: The sensing of bacterial and viral DNA in the cytosol of infected cells is a key initiating event in inflammasome activation and in the production of type I IFN.
source: The sensing of bacterial and viral DNA in the cytosol of infected cells is a key initiating event in inflammasome activation and in the production of type I IFN, which is required for a robust DDR.
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge.

claim: The DDR is initiated by proteins that directly bind to DNA DSBs such as Ku70 and Ku80, which activate DNA-PKcs, and the MRN complex, which activates ATM.
source: The DDR is initiated by proteins that directly bind to DNA DSBs such as Ku70 and Ku80, which activate DNA-PKcs and the MRN complex, which activates ATM (Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about DDR mechanisms and cites prior work.

claim: DDR proteins bind to DNA DSBs in a sequence-independent fashion and are capable of binding mammalian, bacterial and viral DNA.
source: These proteins have been shown to bind to DNA DSBs in a sequence-independent fashion and are capable of binding mammalian, bacterial and viral DNA.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about DDR protein function.

claim: Several DDR proteins have been implicated as sensors for type I IFN production in response to cytosolic bacterial or viral DNA in some settings.
source: In some settings, several of these proteins have been implicated as sensors for type I IFN production in response to cytosolic bacterial or viral DNA (Chatzinikolaou et al., 2014; Lilley et al., 2007) or can couple with known innate immune adaptors to stimulate the production of pro-IL-1β downstream of NF-κB activation (Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: DDR proteins can couple with known innate immune adaptors to stimulate the production of pro-IL-1β downstream of NF-κB activation.
source: In some settings, several of these proteins have been implicated as sensors for type I IFN production in response to cytosolic bacterial or viral DNA (Chatzinikolaou et al., 2014; Lilley et al., 2007) or can couple with known innate immune adaptors to stimulate the production of pro-IL-1β downstream of NF-κB activation (Roth et al., 2014).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: DDR proteins can regulate macrophage function by activating a DDR downstream of genomic DNA DSBs.
source: We show here, however, that these proteins can regulate macrophage function by activating a DDR downstream of genomic DNA DSBs.
evidence: Supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: In activated macrophages, DDR activation by LPS and IFN-γ depends on the production of type I IFN and on Mre11.
source: In activated macrophages, DDR activation by LPS and IFN-γ depends on the production of type I IFN and on the MRN component, Mre11.
evidence: Supported by experiments with Ifnar1-/- and Mre11ATLD1/ATLD1 BMDMs (Figures 3-4).

claim: In activated macrophages, Mre11 functions to activate DDR to genomic DSBs and not as a sensor of bacterial or viral DNA.
source: In this setting, Mre11 functions to activate DDR to genomic DSBs and not as a sensor of bacterial or viral DNA.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental context showing DDR activation by endogenous genomic DSBs.

claim: The activation of the inflammasome by MSU and nigericin depends on ATM and DNA-PKcs, despite the fact that neither of these stimuli include pathogen DNA.
source: Moreover, we show that the activation of the inflammasome by MSU and nigericin depends on ATM and DNA-PKcs, despite the fact that neither of these stimuli include pathogen DNA.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data showing reduced IL-1β in DDR-deficient BMDMs treated with MSU or nigericin (Figure 6D).

claim: In most cell types, ATM is the predominant kinase that mediates DDR.
source: In most cell types, ATM is the predominant kinase that mediates DDR.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about DDR mechanisms.

claim: In macrophages, full activation of the DDR depends on both ATM and DNA-PKcs.
source: In macrophages, however, we find that full activation of the DDR depends on both ATM and DNA-PKcs.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing that both kinases are required for full DDR (Figures 1, 5-7).

claim: The DDR regulates the expression of a variety of chemokine genes in activated macrophages.
source: The DDR regulates the expression of a variety of chemokine genes in activated macrophages.
evidence: Supported by gene expression profiling and qRT-PCR data (Figures 5A-B).

claim: CCL2 mediates inflammatory monocyte trafficking into peripheral tissues.
source: This includes CCL2, which mediates inflammatory monocyte trafficking into peripheral tissues, CCL3 (MIP-1α), CCL4 (MIP-1β), and CXCL1, which regulate the migration of innate immune cells such as macrophages, neutrophils, and NK cells (Griffith et al., 2014; Kuziel et al., 1997).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: CCL3 (MIP-1α), CCL4 (MIP-1β), and CXCL1 regulate the migration of innate immune cells such as macrophages, neutrophils, and NK cells.
source: This includes CCL2, which mediates inflammatory monocyte trafficking into peripheral tissues, CCL3 (MIP-1α), CCL4 (MIP-1β), and CXCL1, which regulate the migration of innate immune cells such as macrophages, neutrophils, and NK cells (Griffith et al., 2014; Kuziel et al., 1997).
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge and cites prior work.

claim: NF-κB is a critical transcription factor that regulates chemokine gene expression downstream of pattern recognition receptors as well as IL-1 and TNF receptors.
source: NF-κB is a critical transcription factor that regulates chemokine gene expression downstream of pattern recognition receptors as well as IL-1 and TNF receptors.
evidence: Draws from established immunological knowledge.

claim: DNA damage can lead to the ATM-dependent activation of NF-κB.
source: DNA damage can also lead to the ATM-dependent activation of NF-κB (Huang et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: It is possible that DDR in activated macrophages regulate chemokine gene expression by augmenting NF-κB activation.
source: Thus, it is possible that DDR in activated macrophages regulate chemokine gene expression by augmenting NF-κB activation.
evidence: Speculative inference based on known NF-κB regulation by DDR.

claim: Cxcl1 expression is regulated by NF-κB and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)-1.
source: Moreover, Cxcl1 expression is regulated by NF-κB and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)−1, which is activated by DNA damage and has a broad range of functions in DDR (Amiri and Richmond, 2003; Nirodi et al., 2001; Rouleau et al., 2010).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: PARP-1 is activated by DNA damage and has a broad range of functions in DDR.
source: Moreover, Cxcl1 expression is regulated by NF-κB and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP)−1, which is activated by DNA damage and has a broad range of functions in DDR (Amiri and Richmond, 2003; Nirodi et al., 2001; Rouleau et al., 2010).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: In activated macrophages, the initiation of a DDR may regulate the genetic program through multiple signaling and transcription pathways.
source: Thus, in activated macrophages, the initiation of a DDR may regulate the genetic program through multiple signaling and transcription pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the discussion of NF-κB and PARP-1 regulation.

claim: The DDR-regulated genetic program in activated macrophages shares functional similarities with the ATM-dependent genetic program in developing pre-B lymphocytes.
source: The DDR-regulated genetic program in activated macrophages shares functional similarities with the ATM-dependent genetic program in developing pre-B lymphocytes (Bednarski et al., 2016; Bredemeyer et al., 2008).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of findings with prior published work cited in the text.

claim: CD69 is regulated by DDR in both pre-B cells undergoing antigen receptor rearrangement and in activated macrophages.
source: CD69, which has an established role in cell homing and migration, is regulated by DDR in both pre-B cells undergoing antigen receptor rearrangement and in activated macrophages.
evidence: Supported by current data and comparison to prior published work.

claim: Many of the DDR-regulated genes in both developing lymphocytes and activated macrophages have an established role in cell migration.
source: Indeed, many of the DDR-regulated genes in both developing lymphocytes and activated macrophages have an established role in cell migration.
evidence: Inferred from analysis of gene functions in both cell types.

claim: Expression of CD69, CD62L, and SWAP70, known to function in lymphocyte migration, are dependent on the DDR signaling in developing B cells.
source: Similarly, expression of CD69, CD62L, and SWAP70, known to function in lymphocyte migration, are dependent on the DDR signaling in developing B cells (Bredemeyer et al., 2008).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: The DDR factor PAXIP1 regulates egress of mature single positive T cells from the thymus.
source: Additionally, the DDR factor PAXIP1 was found to regulate egress of mature single positive T cells from the thymus (Callen et al., 2012).
evidence: Draws from prior published work cited in the text.

claim: DNA DSBs and the resulting DDR influence the homing and migration of various immune cell types in a variety of distinct cellular contexts.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that DNA DSBs and the resulting DDR influence the homing and migration of various immune cell types in a variety of distinct cellular contexts.
evidence: Inferred from the collective findings in macrophages and lymphocytes.

claim: The DDR in macrophages is required, at least in part, for the conversion of pro-caspase 1 to active caspase-1.
source: This is due, at least in part, to a role for the DDR in the conversion of pro-caspase 1 to active caspase-1.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data showing reduced caspase-1 activation in DDR-deficient BMDMs (Figure 6B).

claim: ATM and DNA-PKcs may have distinct activities in the generation of IL-18 and IL-1β.
source: Thus, ATM and DNA-PKcs may have distinct activities in the generation of IL-18 and IL-1β.
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirements for these kinases in IL-18 versus IL-1β production.

claim: Type I IFN is not required solely for the role in promoting the production of the DNA damaging agent, NO.
source: This is not due solely to the role of type I IFN in promoting the production of the DNA damaging agent, NO nor is it due to a requirement for type I IFN to promote DNA DSBs in response to DNA damaging agents.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing IFN-γ rescues NO but not DDR in Ifnar1-/- BMDMs (Figures 4A-B).

claim: Type I IFN is not required to promote DNA DSBs in response to DNA damaging agents.
source: This is not due solely to the role of type I IFN in promoting the production of the DNA damaging agent, NO nor is it due to a requirement for type I IFN to promote DNA DSBs in response to DNA damaging agents.
evidence: Supported by comet assay data showing no difference in DSBs with or without IFN-β (Figure 4C).

claim: It is unclear how type I IFN enables DDR in macrophages.
source: Although it is unclear how type I IFN enables at DDR in macrophages it does not regulate the expression of key DDR proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated as an unresolved question based on the experimental findings.

claim: It is conceivable that type I IFN activates pathways that permit robust DDR in cells expressing limiting amounts of DDR proteins.
source: Thus, it is conceivable that type I IFN activates pathways that permit robust DDR in cells expressing limiting amounts of DDR proteins.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the observation of lower DDR protein expression in BMDMs.

claim: Type I IFN signaling may lead to widespread chromatin modifications induced by type I IFN-dependent gene expression changes.
source: This could result from widespread chromatin modifications induced by type I IFN-dependent gene expression changes.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about mechanism of type I IFN effect on DDR.

claim: Type I IFN-induced chromatin modifications may enhance DDR activation to DSBs without increasing DNA DSBs.
source: Importantly, we find that this does not lead to an increase in DNA DSBs. However, these chromatin modifications may enhance DDR activation to DSBs (Bakkenist and Kastan, 2003; Floyd et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on prior published work about chromatin and DDR.
